title: Germany’s firewall against the AfD isn’t working
gist: The AfD took 43.8 per cent in Saxony-Anhalt against the CDU's 17.2 per cent and leads national polls at 28 per cent, seven points clear of CDU/CSU. Hussain argues Germany's Brandmauer now works against its own purpose — it hands the AfD electoral authority without governing responsibility, which is why it has radicalised rather than moderated — and that Merz's imitation strategy cut irregular migration but transferred the electoral reward to the AfD.

insights.claim: The AfD won 43.8 per cent of the popular vote in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its share from the 2021 state election, while the CDU — which had governed the state since 2002 — came a distant second on 17.2 per cent.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: A 24-year incumbent party losing a state by 26 points marks a step-change in German political risk, not a protest blip.
insights.locator: The AfD won 43.8 per cent of the popular vote

insights.claim: The AfD is leading nationwide polls at 28 per cent, seven percentage points ahead of the CDU/CSU, so its strength is not confined to one eastern state.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: A seven-point national lead for a party under extremism surveillance is the core German political-risk datapoint to track into the next federal cycle.
insights.quote: The AfD is leading nationwide polls at 28 per cent, seven percentage points ahead of the CDU/CSU.
insights.locator: Nor is its success confined to one eastern state.

insights.claim: The AfD's trajectory runs from 12.6 per cent on entering the Bundestag in 2017 to first place in Thuringia in 2024 to near-half the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, a progression that makes the protest-movement description untenable.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Support has converted from protest into a durable political option, which raises the probability of eventual coalition inclusion.
insights.locator: For years, it was possible to describe the party as a protest movement.

insights.claim: Excluding the AfD from coalitions gives it the best of both worlds — the authority of having won an election plus freedom from the responsibility of governing — so it never has to reconcile mass deportations, cheaper energy and cultural renewal with legal scrutiny or an ageing nation's dependence on foreign workers.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Quarantine strategies preserve insurgent purity; the analytical implication is that exclusion raises, not lowers, the AfD's long-run ceiling.
insights.quote: The AfD alone can remain politically pure, never dirtied by compromise, budgets or having to deliver what it promised.
insights.locator: Under this scenario, it does not have to explain

insights.claim: Protection from the consequences of power helps explain why the AfD has become more radical as it has grown more popular, inverting the pattern elsewhere in Europe where far-right parties moderated as government came within reach.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Breaks the standard 'power moderates' assumption for Germany — expect escalation, not convergence, as AfD support rises.

insights.claim: Keeping the AfD out of office in Saxony-Anhalt requires assembling another awkward coalition of parties with little in common, united by what they oppose rather than what they want, and if that government struggles the AfD simply says it told you so.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Unstable negative-coalition governance is the base case in eastern states, feeding the next AfD advance.
insights.locator: But to keep the AfD out, its opponents will have to assemble

insights.claim: Germany's institutional alertness to the far right has descended into ritual — shock, condemnation, another promise nobody will work with the AfD — language that reassures those inside the democratic consensus but does nothing to reach those who have left it.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Signals the mainstream has no working persuasion strategy, which is the condition for continued far-right gains.
insights.locator: At the same time, Germany’s institutional alertness

insights.claim: Worse, ritual firewall rhetoric lets established parties frame protecting democracy as indistinguishable from protecting themselves, which feeds the very anti-establishment grievance driving AfD support.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing loop: anti-extremism messaging that reads as incumbency defence accelerates the insurgency.
insights.locator: Worse, it allows the established parties to frame

insights.claim: Merz borrowed AfD rhetoric and accepted its premise that reducing migration is the overriding measure of government success, introducing stricter border controls, accelerated deportations and limits on family reunification — irregular migration fell, but the electoral reward went to the AfD.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that policy convergence on immigration does not reclaim far-right voters; it legitimises the challenger's framing.
insights.quote: Far from weakening the far right, Merz has helped legitimise its framing and left voters with a choice between the real thing and a more cautious imitation.
insights.locator: Imitating the AfD is no answer.

insights.claim: Merz described migration as a “problem in the cityscape” and told critics to “ask your daughters” what he meant, an escalation of rhetoric that accompanied the strategy's failure.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Rhetorical escalation by a mainstream chancellor marks how far the Overton window has moved in Germany.
insights.quote: Merz even described migration as a “problem in the cityscape” before telling critics to “ask your daughters” what he meant.
insights.locator: He has introduced stricter border controls

insights.claim: The German experience carries a direct lesson for Labour and the Conservatives, both of which have toughened immigration rhetoric in response to Nigel Farage and Reform UK: voters rarely reward the imitation.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Predicts UK mainstream parties' current anti-immigration triangulation will fail to dent Reform, keeping UK political fragmentation risk elevated.
insights.locator: There is a lesson for Britain’s two parties

themes.theme: What is actually driving eastern Germany

insights.claim: Migration alone does not explain eastern Germany's struggles: Saxony-Anhalt has experienced industrial decline, an ageing population and the departure of many younger residents, beneath which sits a feeling that decisions are made elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Demographic and industrial decay, not immigration, is the underlying driver — so immigration policy alone cannot defuse the political risk.
insights.locator: Migration alone does not explain the struggles

insights.claim: The AfD's core competence is narrative aggregation: it gathers economic stagnation, migration, green policies, the war in Ukraine and distrust of Berlin into a single story that ordinary Germans have lost control of their country.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Explains why green transition costs and Ukraine support are politically coupled in Germany — both feed the same grievance bundle.
insights.locator: The AfD has become skilled at gathering these different grievances

insights.claim: The Saxony-Anhalt AfD branch has been classified as right-wing extremist by the state's domestic intelligence agency, and its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund campaigned on a deportation offensive, banning rainbow flags in schools and replacing the state slogan “Think Modern” with “Think German”.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: Documents that the strongest-performing AfD branch is also the most extreme, which constrains any mainstream accommodation.
insights.locator: The Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified as right-wing extremist

insights.claim: Dismissing every AfD voter as extremist evades the question of why so many people no longer believe the other parties are listening to them, and some of the underlying grievances are real.
insights.speaker: Raza Hussain
insights.so_what: The author's prescription — compete with and defeat AfD ideas rather than quarantine them — is the test to apply to any mainstream German strategy announcement.
insights.locator: Some of these grievances are real.
